claim: The ventral tail striatum (vTS) is located close to the basolateral and central nuclei of the amygdala.
source: To access the vTS, a deep brain area close to the basolateral - and central nuclei of the amygdala, we used miniature-microscope Ca2+ imaging (Figure 1B and C; Ghosh et al., 2011).
evidence: The text explicitly states the anatomical location of the vTS relative to amygdalar structures, supported by citation to Ghosh et al., 2011.

claim: The Drd1aCre mouse line (EY217 from GenSAT) shows expression of Cre in the vTS but not in adjacent cortical or claustrum structures.
source: The Drd1aCremouse chosen for this purpose (line EY217 from GenSAT; see Materials and methods) shows expression of Cre in the vTS, but no expression was observed in the adjacent cortical or claustrum structures (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; see also Gerfen et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by direct observation documented in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and corroborated by citation to Gerfen et al., 2013.

claim: 45 out of 163 imaged D1R+ neurons responded to footshocks with robust Ca2+ signals.
source: One day later, each of the six CS blocks was followed by a 1 s footshock, to which 45/163 imaged D1R+ neurons responded with robust Ca2+ signals (Figure 1F and H).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1F and H.

claim: The number of D1R+ neurons responding to tone beeps increased during the training session compared to habituation.
source: During this training session, an increased number of D1R+ neurons responded to tone beeps (CS) (Figure 1J and L; Chi-square test, p=0.018, Χ2df=2 = 8.004)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Chi-square test) and data visualization in Figure 1J and L.

claim: The average Z-scored Ca2+ signal of tone-responsive D1R+ neurons was increased during the fear memory recall session compared to the training session.
source: the average Z-scored Ca2+ signal was increased above the response amplitude on the training session (Figure 1J and K; 0.366±0.071 vs 0.093±0.034 for n=19 and 17 responders, respectively; 95% CI: [0.2164; 0.516]; [0.0212; 0.1649]; p=0.001, U=61, Mann-Whitney test).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data with statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney test) and visualization in Figure 1J and K.

claim: A sub-population of D1R+ vTS neurons responds to movement-ON transitions.
source: Aligning GCaMP6m fluorescence traces to the movement onset revealed Ca2+ events in a sub- population of D1R+ neurons; we call these 'movement-ON' responses.
evidence: The claim is based on direct observation from Ca2+ imaging data analysis.

claim: The number of D1R+ neurons responding to movement-ON transitions during CS presentations increased during the training session and was maintained at an elevated level during the recall session.
source: The analysis showed that the number of D1R+ neurons that responded to a movement-ON transition during the time of the CS presentations increased during the training session, and was maintained at an elevated level during the recall session (Figure 1S, filled symbols; p=0.0155, Χ2df=2 = 8.340, Chi-square test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Chi-square test) and data shown in Figure 1S.

claim: The activity of D1R+ neurons in the vTS is higher during movement than during freezing on most sessions.
source: Pairwise comparisons of these conditional Ca2+ event frequencies within each session showed that on most sessions, the activity of D1R+ neurons was significantly higher when the mice moved, than when they froze, with the exception of the no-CS times on the training day (Figure 1U; Dunn's multiple comparisons test; for p-values, see legend to Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Dunn's multiple comparisons test) and data visualization in Figure 1U.

claim: On the training day, the Ca2+ event frequency of D1R+ neurons was significantly increased by the CS when mice were moving.
source: On the training day, given that mice moved, the Ca2+ event frequency was significantly increased by the CS (Figure 1U; p=0.0163, Mean rank difference = 241.9, Kruskal-Wallis test followed by Dunn's multiple comparisons test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Kruskal-Wallis test followed by Dunn's multiple comparisons test) and data shown in Figure 1U.

claim: Footshock- and tone-responding D1R+ neurons are located in a hotspot in the posterior-ventral region of the tail striatum medial to the LA.
source: This revealed a hotspot of footshock- and tone-responding D1R+ neurons in the posterior-ventral region of the tail striatum medial to the LA (Figure 2A and B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on spatial mapping of imaged neurons shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: During the habituation session, neurons with responses to the CS and movement did not strongly overlap in D1R+ vTS neurons.
source: Venn plots of the overlay of the various response types showed that during the habituation session, neurons with responses to the CS and movement did not strongly overlap, and represented a small proportion of the imaged neurons (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: During the recall session, tone- and movement-ON responders in D1R+ vTS neurons overlapped substantially.
source: During the recall session, the populations of both tone - and movement responders stayed constant with respect to the training day, and these response types now overlapped substantially (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: About forty percent of Adora+ vTS neurons responded to footshocks presented during the training session.
source: About forty percent of the Adora+ vTS neurons responded to footshocks presented during the training session (79/201 neurons; Figure 3C and E).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with quantitative data and supported by Figure 3C and E.

claim: A small subpopulation (~8%) of Adora+ vTS neurons responded to tone beeps during the CS.
source: A small subpopulation (13/173 or ~8%) responded to tone beeps during the CS (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with quantitative data and supported by Figure 3F.

claim: The percentage of tone (CS)-responsive Adora+ neurons did not change during fear learning.
source: Contrasting with the D1R+ neurons, the percentage of tone (CS)-responsive neurons did not change during fear learning (Figure 3F–H; Figure 3I; p=0.415, Χ2df=2 = 1.756, Chi-square test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Chi-square test) and data shown in Figure 3F-H and 3I.

claim: The number of Adora+ neurons showing movement-ON responses in the absence of a CS decreased over the course of fear learning.
source: In the absence of tones, a moderate sub-population of Adora+ neurons showed movement-ON responses during the habituation session (27/173 or ~16 %); this number decreased over the course of fear learning (Figure 3J–L; Figure 3P, open symbols; p=0.0229, Χ2df=2 = 7.557; Chi-square test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Chi-square test) and data shown in Figure 3J-L and 3P.

claim: The number of Adora+ neurons showing movement-ON responses during the CS was unchanged over the three-day fear learning protocol.
source: In contrast, during the CS, there was a larger number of Adora+ neurons that showed movement-ON responses; their number was unchanged over the three-day fear learning protocol (Figure 3M–O; Figure 3P, closed symbols; p=0.717, Χ2df=2 = 0.67; Chi-square test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Chi-square test) and data shown in Figure 3M-O and 3P.

claim: During all three behavior sessions, the activity of Adora+ neurons was larger during movement than during freezing, irrespective of the presence or absence of a CS.
source: During all three behavior sessions, and irrespective of the presence or absence of a CS, the activity of Adora+ neurons was larger during movement than during freezing (Figure 3R; see legend to Figure 3—figure supplement 3 for the corresponding p-values; post-hoc Dunn's multiple comparison test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Dunn's multiple comparison test) and data shown in Figure 3R.

claim: The presence or absence of a CS did not significantly modulate the activity of Adora+ neurons, irrespective of whether the mice moved or froze.
source: On the other hand, the presence or absence of a CS did not significantly modulate the activity of Adora+ neurons, irrespective of whether the mice moved, or froze (Figure 3R; see legend to Figure 3—figure supplement 3 for p-values; post-hoc Dunn's multiple comparison test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Dunn's multiple comparison test) and data shown in Figure 3R.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of Adora+ neurons in the vTS did not lead to changes in the movement activity of naive mice.
source: Optogenetic stimulation did not lead to changes in the movement activity of the Adora2aCre mice, nor of the Drd1aCre mice (Figure 4B and C; N=8 and 7 mice; p>0.999, W=0, and p=0.837, t6=0.215, Wilcoxon and paired t-test, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon and paired t-test) and data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of D1R+ neurons in the vTS did not lead to changes in the movement activity of naive mice.
source: Optogenetic stimulation did not lead to changes in the movement activity of the Adora2aCre mice, nor of the Drd1aCre mice (Figure 4B and C; N=8 and 7 mice; p>0.999, W=0, and p=0.837, t6=0.215, Wilcoxon and paired t-test, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon and paired t-test) and data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: In naive mice, the activity of neither D1R+ nor Adora+ neurons is sufficient to modulate the movement activity of the mice.
source: These experiments suggest that in naive mice, the activity of neither D1R+ - nor of Adora+ neurons is sufficient to modulate the movement activity of the mice.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the optogenetic stimulation results presented in Figure 4.

claim: Freezing levels were not different between the Arch- and the control group during the training day, neither for the CS- nor for the no-CS epochs.
source: This showed that freezing levels were not different between the Arch- and the control group, neither for the CS- nor for the no-CS epochs (Figure 5E, left, for the CS epochs: p=0.338, F1,20 = 0.965; Figure 5E right, for the no-CS epochs: p=0.454, F1,20=0.583; two-way repeated measures - ANOVA).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (two-way repeated measures ANOVA) and data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Optogenetic silencing of D1R+ neurons during footshocks did not change the freezing behavior of mice during the training day.
source: Thus, optogenetic silencing of the footshock-evoked activity of D1R+ vTS neurons did not change the freezing behavior of mice during the training day.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analysis of freezing data during training (Figure 5E).

claim: There was a significant difference in CS-driven freezing between control and Arch-expressing Drd1aCre mice during fear memory recall.
source: Averaging and statistical analysis revealed a significant difference in CS-driven freezing between control - and Arch-expressing Drd1aCre mice (Figure 5G, closed data points; p=0.040, F1,20=4.853, two-way repeated measures - ANOVA).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (two-way repeated measures ANOVA) and data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Freezing during the no-CS epochs was unchanged between control and Arch-expressing Drd1aCre mice during fear memory recall.
source: On the other hand, freezing during the no-CS epochs was unchanged between the two groups (Figure 5G, open data points; p=0.662, F1,20=0.197 two-way repeated measures - ANOVA).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (two-way repeated measures ANOVA) and data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of D1R+ neurons in the vTS during footshocks causes a diminished auditory-cued recall of fear memory 1 day later.
source: Thus, optogenetic inhibition of D1R+ neurons in the vTS during the footshocks on the training day causes a diminished auditory-cued recall of fear memory 1 day later.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analysis of freezing data during recall (Figure 5G).

claim: Footshock-driven activity of D1R+ vTS neurons contributes to auditory-cued fear learning.
source: These data suggest that footshock-driven activity of D1R+ vTS neurons contributes to auditory-cued fear learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic silencing experiments (Figure 5).

claim: Freezing levels were not different between the Arch- and the eGFP groups on the training day for Adora+ neuron silencing experiments.
source: The analysis of freezing during the CS- and no-CS epochs revealed no differences in the freezing levels between the Arch- and the eGFP groups on the training day (Figure 6E; p=0.528, F1, 17 = 0.415 and p=0.312, F1,17 = 1.087, respectively; two-way repeated measures ANOVA).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (two-way repeated measures ANOVA) and data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Footshock-driven activity in Adora+ vTS neurons is not necessary for the freezing behavior that develops during the training day.
source: Thus, similar as for the D1R+ neurons, footshock-driven activity in Adora+ vTS neurons is not necessary for the freezing behavior that develops during the training day.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analysis of freezing data during training (Figure 6E).

claim: There was a trend towards increased freezing during the no-CS epochs in the Arch group compared to eGFP controls during fear memory recall for Adora+ neuron silencing.
source: This showed a trend towards an increased freezing during the no-CS epochs in the Arch group as compared to eGFP controls, although this difference did not reach statistical significance (Figure 6G, right; p=0.0512, F1,17 = 4.40; two-way repeated measures ANOVA, N=8 and 11 eGFP and Arch mice, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (two-way repeated measures ANOVA) and data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Freezing during the CS epochs was unchanged between the Arch and the control group during fear memory recall for Adora+ neuron silencing.
source: On the other hand, freezing during the CS epochs was unchanged between the Arch and the control group (Figure 6G, left; p=0.624, F1,17 = 0.249; two-way repeated measures ANOVA).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (two-way repeated measures ANOVA) and data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Silencing the footshock-driven activity of Adora+ neurons in the vTS induces a trend towards higher freezing during fear memory recall in the absence of the CS.
source: Thus, silencing the footshock-driven activity of Adora+ neurons in the vTS induces a trend towards higher freezing during fear memory recall in the absence of the CS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analysis of freezing data during recall (Figure 6G).

claim: Direct and indirect pathway neurons of the vTS have separate, but functionally synergistic roles in fear learning.
source: These findings, together with the results obtained from silencing D1R+ vTS neurons (see above), suggest that direct and indirect pathway neurons of the vTS have separate, but functionally synergistic roles in fear learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results of optogenetic silencing experiments on both D1R+ and Adora+ neurons (Figures 5 and 6).

claim: The action of both D1R+ and Adora+ vTS subsystems together increases the difference between the strength of a defensive behavior in the presence and absence of a learned sensory cue.
source: In fact, the action of both sub-systems together increases the difference between the strength of a defensive behavior in the presence, and absence of a learned sensory cue.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results of optogenetic silencing experiments on both D1R+ and Adora+ neurons (Figures 5 and 6).

claim: The highest number and density of backlabeled cells in both Drd1aCre and Adora2aCre mice were found in the secondary somatosensory cortex (S2) and in the dorsal (granular and dysgranular) part of the insular cortex (InsCx).
source: In both Drd1aCre and Adora2aCre mice, we found the highest number and density of backlabeled cells in the secondary somatosensory cortex (S2), and in the dorsal (granular and dysgranular) part of the insular cortex (InsCx; see also Figure 7—source data 2 for a list of all brain structures with detected presynaptic neurons; Figure 7C, D, G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by rabies virus tracing data shown in Figure 7C, D, G and H.

claim: Structures known to process auditory- and multimodal sensory information were more strongly back-labeled in Adora2aCre mice than in Drd1aCre mice.
source: Thus, we found that structures known to process auditory- and multimodal sensory information, like the auditory cortex (AUD), the temporal association cortex (TeA), the posterior triangular thalamic nucleus (PoT), the posterior intralaminar thalamic nucleus (PiL) and the basolateral amygdala (BLA), were more strongly back-labeled in Adora2aCre mice than in Drd1aCre mice (Figure 7G and H; Figure 7—figure supplement 3; LeDoux, 2000; Weinberger, 2007; Sacco and Sacchetti, 2010; Dalmay et al., 2019; Barsy et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by rabies virus tracing data shown in Figure 7G and H, and corroborated by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Rabies-virus mediated circuit tracing shows that the vTS receives its main cortical input from the S2 and the InsCx, followed by primary somatosensory areas.
source: Taken together, rabies-virus mediated circuit tracing shows that the vTS receives its main cortical input from the S2 and the InsCx, followed by primary somatosensory areas.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rabies virus tracing experiments (Figure 7).

claim: Blue light pulses at maximal light intensity evoked robust optogenetically-evoked EPSCs of 8.8±1.6 nA in D1R+ vTS neurons.
source: Blue light pulses (1ms) at maximal light intensity evoked robust optogenetically-evoked EPSCs of 8.8±1.6 nA in D1R+ vTS neurons (95% CI: [5.28 nA; 12.2 nA]; n=12 cells)
evidence: The claim is directly stated with quantitative data from optogenetic circuit mapping experiments.

claim: Blue light pulses at maximal light intensity evoked optogenetically-evoked EPSCs of 2.5±0.5 nA in Adora+ vTS neurons.
source: and of 2.5±0.5 nA in Adora+ vTS neurons (95% CI: [1.49 nA; 3.58 nA], n=19 cells)
evidence: The claim is directly stated with quantitative data from optogenetic circuit mapping experiments.

claim: The EPSC amplitudes from pInsCx to vTS neurons were significantly different between D1R+ and Adora+ neurons.
source: the EPSC amplitudes were significantly different between the two types of principal neurons (p=0.002, U=40, Mann-Whitney test; Figure 8C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney test) and data shown in Figure 8C-E.

claim: The paired-pulse ratio (PPR) at pInsCx to vTS synapses did not differ between D1R+ and Adora+ neuron types.
source: The paired-pulse ratio (PPR) did not differ between the two neuron types (Figure 8F; p=0.208, t28=1.288, ; unpaired t-test; 95% CI: [0.637; 0.827] and [0.711; 0.960] for D1R+ and Adora+ neurons).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (unpaired t-test) and data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: The ratio of direct excitation over feedforward inhibition was significantly smaller in Adora+ vTS neurons as compared to D1R+ neurons.
source: On the other hand, the ratio of direct excitation over feedforward inhibition was significantly smaller in Adora+ vTS neurons as compared to D1R+ neurons (Figure 8—figure supplement 1; p=0.0054, U=31, Mann-Whitney test; 95% CI: [2.19; 4.10] and [1.05; 2.40] for D1R+ and Adora+ neurons).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney test) and data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both D1R+ and Adora+ neurons of the vTS receive robust excitatory inputs from the pInsCx.
source: Taken together, optogenetically-assisted circuit mapping shows that both D1R+ and Adora+ neurons of the vTS receive robust excitatory inputs from the pInsCx.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic circuit mapping experiments (Figure 8).

claim: The pInsCx provides an important cortical input to the vTS.
source: This, together with the monosynaptic rabies tracing (Figure 7), identifies the pInsCx as providing an important cortical inputs to the vTS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results of rabies tracing (Figure 7) and optogenetic circuit mapping (Figure 8).

claim: Optogenetically evoked EPSCs at the pInsCx to D1R+ vTS connection showed a significant increase of the AMPA/NMDA ratio in the CS+US group compared to the CS-only group.
source: Optogenetically evoked EPSCs at the pInsCx to D1R+ vTS connection showed a significant increase of the AMPA/NMDA ratio in the CS+US group, as compared to the CS-only group, suggesting that at this connection, a postsynaptic form of LTP had occurred during fear learning (Figure 9B and D; p=0.001, t21=3.833, unpaired t-test; 95% CI: [1.687; 2.764] and [3.128; 4.719] for CS-only and CS+US).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (unpaired t-test) and data shown in Figure 9B and D.

claim: The PPR was unchanged in D1R+ neurons after fear learning.
source: The PPR, however, was unchanged in D1R+ neurons (Figure 9C and D; p=0.974, t21=0.033, unpaired t-test; 95% CI: [0.448; 0.765] and [0.429; 0.791] for CS-only and CS+US).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (unpaired t-test) and data shown in Figure 9C and D.

claim: At the pInsCx to Adora+ vTS connection, the AMPA/NMDA ratio was unchanged after fear learning.
source: Conversely, at the pInsCx to Adora+ vTS connection, the AMPA/NMDA ratio was unchanged (Figure 9E and G; p=0.162, t22=1.445, unpaired t-test; 95% CI: [1.538; 2.896] and [0.946; 2.251] for CS-only and CS+US)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (unpaired t-test) and data shown in Figure 9E and G.

claim: The PPR was increased in the CS+US group compared to the CS-only group at the pInsCx to Adora+ vTS connection.
source: but instead, the PPR was increased in the CS+US group as compared to the CS-only group (Figure 9F and G; p=0.001, U=18, Mann-Whitney test; 95% CI: [0.193; 0.582] and [0.574; 0.938] for CS-only and CS+US).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney test) and data shown in Figure 9F and G.

claim: Fear learning induces a presynaptic form of long-term depression at the pInsCx to Adora+ vTS synapse.
source: The latter finding suggests that fear learning induces a presynaptic form of long-term depression at the pInsCx to Adora+ vTS synapse.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of PPR changes at the pInsCx to Adora+ vTS synapse (Figure 9F and G).

claim: Auditory-cued fear learning drives long-term plasticity with opposite outcomes at cortical synapses onto D1R+ and Adora+ neurons in the vTS.
source: Thus, auditory-cued fear learning drives long-term plasticity with opposite outcomes at cortical synapses onto D1R+ and Adora+ neurons in the vTS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results of plasticity measurements at pInsCx synapses onto both D1R+ and Adora+ neurons (Figure 9).

claim: The differential forms of long-term plasticity at pInsCx synapses might contribute to the complementary roles of the two types of vTS principal neurons in fear learning.
source: These differential forms of long-term plasticity might contribute to the complementary roles of the two types of vTS principal neurons in fear learning.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the combined results of plasticity measurements and behavioral experiments.

claim: The amygdala has an important role in fear learning.
source: Studies spanning several decades have firmly established that the amygdala has an important role in fear learning (see Davis, 1992; LeDoux, 2000; Duvarci and Pare, 2014; Tovote et al., 2015, for reviews).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple review articles.

claim: The lateral amygdala (LA) is viewed as an input structure to the amygdalar complex.
source: The lateral amygdala (LA) is viewed as an input structure to the amygdalar complex (LeDoux et al., 1990)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to LeDoux et al., 1990.

claim: The execution of learned freezing depends on a central amygdala to midbrain (periaqueductal gray) projection.
source: Finally, the execution of learned freezing depends on a central amygdala to midbrain (periaqueductal gray) projection (LeDoux et al., 1988; Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to LeDoux et al., 1988 and Tovote et al., 2016.

claim: The striatum is part of the basal ganglia motor system.
source: The striatum is part of the basal ganglia motor system, a neuronal system with important roles in the control of movement, action selection, and reward-based learning (for reviews, see Hikosaka et al., 2000; Graybiel, 2005; Grillner et al., 2005; Redgrave et al., 2010; Nelson and Kreitzer, 2014; Klaus et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple review articles.

claim: Striato-nigral neurons project in a direct pathway to basal ganglia output structures and selectively express D1-dopamine receptors (D1R).
source: First, striato-nigral neurons project in a direct pathway to basal ganglia output structures like the Substantia nigra pars reticularis and others; these neurons selectively express D1-dopamine receptors (D1R).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about striatal neuron types.

claim: Striato-pallidal neurons project in a more indirect pathway towards the basal ganglia output structures and selectively express D2-dopamine receptors and adenosine-2A receptors (Adora).
source: Second, striato-pallidal neurons project in a more indirect pathway towards the basal ganglia output structures; these neurons selectively express D2-dopamine receptors, and also adenosine-2A receptors (Adora) (Gerfen et al., 1990; Schiffmann and Vanderhaeghen, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gerfen et al., 1990 and Schiffmann and Vanderhaeghen, 1993.

claim: The dorsal striatum is involved in the learning of motor sequences and in the selection of appropriate actions.
source: The dorsal striatum is involved in the learning of motor sequences and in the selection of appropriate actions (Nelson and Kreitzer, 2014; Klaus et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nelson and Kreitzer, 2014 and Klaus et al., 2019.

claim: The ventral striatum is important for reward-based learning.
source: whereas the ventral striatum is important for reward-based learning (Humphries and Prescott, 2010; Cox and Witten, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Humphries and Prescott, 2010 and Cox and Witten, 2019.

claim: A posterior area of the striatum called tail striatum was identified based on brain-wide studies of cortical inputs to the mouse striatum.
source: Recently, based on brain-wide studies of the cortical inputs to the mouse striatum, a further sub-area of the striatum was identified; a posterior area called tail striatum (Hintiryan et al., 2016; Hunnicutt et al., 2016; see Valjent and Gangarossa, 2021 for review).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hintiryan et al., 2016, Hunnicutt et al., 2016, and Valjent and Gangarossa, 2021.

claim: Early in vivo recordings in the LA have found CS- and US-responsive neurons in the tail striatum adjacent to the LA.
source: Interestingly, early in vivo recordings in the LA have found CS- and US-responsive neurons in the tail striatum adjacent to the LA (Romanski et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Romanski et al., 1993.

claim: The tail striatum is composed of D1R-expressing (D1R+) and D2R- and Adora-expressing neurons.
source: Recent work has shown that the tail striatum is, similarly as other striatal areas, composed of D1R-expressing (D1R+) and D2R- and Adora-expressing neurons (Gangarossa et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gangarossa et al., 2019.

claim: Dopaminergic axons in the tail striatum code for salient sensory stimuli, but not for rewarding stimuli.
source: Furthermore, in vivo imaging studies have shown that dopaminergic axons in the tail striatum code for salient sensory stimuli, but not for rewarding stimuli (Menegas et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Menegas et al., 2018.

claim: Yellow light strongly hyperpolarizes Arch-expressing D1R+ and Adora+ vTS neurons and suppresses action potential (AP) firing.
source: We found in ex vivo experiments that yellow light strongly hyperpolarizes Arch-expressing D1R+ and Adora+ vTS neurons, suppresses action potential (AP) firing, and does not evoke rebound APs when the light is switched off (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Yellow light does not evoke rebound APs when switched off in Arch-expressing D1R+ and Adora+ vTS neurons.
source: We found in ex vivo experiments that yellow light strongly hyperpolarizes Arch-expressing D1R+ and Adora+ vTS neurons, suppresses action potential (AP) firing, and does not evoke rebound APs when the light is switched off (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Sex-specific differences exist in the strength and types of learned defensive behaviors in rodents.
source: It has been shown, mainly using rats, that sex-specific differences exist in the strength and types of learned defensive behaviors (Maren et al., 1994; Pryce et al., 1999; Gruene et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Maren et al., 1994, Pryce et al., 1999, and Gruene et al., 2015.

claim: Males in general show higher freezing than females in rodents.
source: In rodents, males in general show higher freezing than females
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about sex differences in fear learning.

claim: Females show a higher degree of fast bouts of escape reactions (called 'darting') in rodents.
source: whereas females show a higher degree of fast bouts of escape reactions (called 'darting'), which can also take the form of learned responses (Gruene et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gruene et al., 2015.

claim: During fear generalization, PTSD patients exhibited stronger responses in the striatum, amygdala and insular cortex amongst other areas.
source: Indeed, it was found that during fear generalization, PTSD patients exhibited stronger responses in the striatum, amygdala and insular cortex amongst other areas (Morey et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Morey et al., 2020.

claim: The pInsCx displays state-dependent signaling relating to physiological needs or to the aversive state of the animal.
source: Recent studies have shown that the pInsCx displays state-dependent signaling relating to physiological needs, or to the aversive state of the animal (Livneh et al., 2017; Gehrlach et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Livneh et al., 2017 and Gehrlach et al., 2019.

claim: A subarea of the pInsCx processes auditory information.
source: Moreover, it was shown that a subarea of the pInsCx processes auditory information (Rodgers et al., 2008; Sawatari et al., 2011; Gogolla et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rodgers et al., 2008, Sawatari et al., 2011, and Gogolla et al., 2014.

claim: A separate set of midbrain dopamine neurons innervates the tail striatum and these dopamine projections are activated by salient, but not by rewarding stimuli.
source: Recent work has shown that a separate set of midbrain dopamine neurons innervates the tail striatum, and that these dopamine projections are activated by salient, but not by rewarding stimuli (Menegas et al., 2015; Menegas et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Menegas et al., 2015 and Menegas et al., 2018.

claim: Dopamine release in the amygdala contributes to fear learning.
source: Classical studies showed that dopamine release in the amygdala contributes to fear learning (Lamont and Kokkinidis, 1998; Guarraci et al., 1999; Nader and LeDoux, 1999)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lamont and Kokkinidis, 1998, Guarraci et al., 1999, and Nader and LeDoux, 1999.

claim: Footshock-driven activity of ventral tegmental area (VTA) dopamine neurons that project to the basal amygdala (BA) contributes to fear learning.
source: and a recent study showed that footshock-driven activity of ventral tegmental area (VTA) dopamine neurons that project to the basal amygdala (BA), contributes to fear learning (Tang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tang et al., 2020.
